latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Aberrant Th2 cell expansion with IL-5, IL-4, IL-13, eotaxin and TSLP signaling drives bone marrow eosinophilopoiesis, prolonged eosinophil survival, and tissue trafficking. Cardinal upstream driver of asthma, blood eosinophilia and tissue eosinophilic infiltration in EGPA.

Activated tissue eosinophils release MBP, ECP, EPO, EDN and form eosinophil extracellular traps, producing direct endothelial, neuronal, myocyte and mucosal cytotoxicity, prothrombotic milieu and tissue remodeling.
Histopathologic hallmark of EGPA: extravascular necrotizing granulomas with central eosinophilic necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes/giant cells in lung, skin, and nerve.

Pauci-immune necrotizing inflammation of small-to-medium arteries, arterioles, capillaries and venules driving purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, GI ischemia, alveolar capillaritis and crescentic GN. Predominates in ANCA+ subset.

In ~30-40% of EGPA, MPO-ANCA primes TNF-activated neutrophils, triggering oxidative burst, NETosis and degranulation against endothelium. Most strongly tied to glomerulonephritis, mononeuritis multiplex, alveolar hemorrhage and purpura phenotypes.
Necrotizing crescentic GN with scant immune deposits; less frequent than in MPA/GPA, predominantly in MPO-ANCA+ EGPA. Causes hematuria, RBC casts, proteinuria and rising creatinine.

Ischemic injury to peripheral nerves from epineurial vasa nervorum vasculitis combined with eosinophil-mediated neurotoxicity, producing painful asymmetric multifocal sensorimotor mononeuropathies (classic peroneal, ulnar, median).

Direct eosinophilic infiltration and degranulation in myocardium produces myocyte necrosis, intramural microvascular vasculitis, intracavitary thrombus and progressive endomyocardial fibrosis (Loeffler-like). Leading cause of EGPA mortality, more frequent in ANCA-negative phenotype.

Combined eosinophilic mucosal/transmural infiltration and small-vessel mesenteric vasculitis causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, GI bleeding, ischemic ulceration and (in severe FFS+ disease) bowel perforation.

Tissue eosinophilic infiltration of alveoli/interstitium produces transient migratory infiltrates, peripheral non-segmental opacities, BAL eosinophilia (>25%), cough and dyspnea distinct from vasculitic alveolar hemorrhage.

Adult-onset, often severe, eosinophilic asthma is the near-universal prodrome of EGPA, typically preceding vasculitis by months to years. Persists during and after vasculitis remission, requiring long-term ICS/LABA.
Chronic eosinophilic rhinosinusitis and nasal polyposis are core ENT prodromal features. Their presence is one of the Five-Factor Score components (absence worsens prognosis).

Eosinophil granule proteins (MBP, ECP) and EETs neutralize heparan sulfate, activate platelets, expose tissue factor and induce thrombomodulin downregulation, producing increased venous thrombosis risk and intracardiac thrombus formation.

Neutrophilic alveolar capillaritis with hemosiderin-laden macrophages producing diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. Less common than in MPA/GPA but clinically catastrophic when present, predominantly in MPO-ANCA+ EGPA.
Systemic IL-6/TNF/IL-1 release with elevated CRP/ESR, fever, weight loss, night sweats and fatigue accompanying active vasculitic phase.
Palpable purpura, subcutaneous nodules, urticaria-like lesions and livedo from leukocytoclastic and eosinophilic cutaneous vasculitis.

Cumulative effect of high-dose glucocorticoids and cytotoxic/B-cell-depleting agents on cellular and humoral immunity, increasing risk of bacterial sepsis, PJP, CMV reactivation, herpes zoster, fungal infection, and HBV reactivation.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-5 expands and prolongs eosinophil survival, driving peripheral eosinophilia (often >1.5x10^9/L, classically >10% of WBC).
Th2/IL-5/IL-13 axis drives airway eosinophilia, smooth muscle hyperresponsiveness and asthma activity.
Same Th2 axis drives chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyposis (CRSwNP) phenotype.
Tissue-recruited activated eosinophils degranulate, releasing MBP/ECP/EPO/EDN and forming EETs.
IL-4/IL-13 drive class-switch to IgE; total IgE is frequently elevated.
Eosinophilic alveolar/interstitial infiltration drives transient pulmonary opacities and BAL eosinophilia >25%.
Eosinophil granule proteins are directly cardiotoxic, producing myocarditis progressing to endomyocardial fibrosis (Loeffler pattern).
Eosinophilic mucosal/transmural infiltration drives gastroenteritis with abdominal pain and diarrhea.
Eosinophil-derived MBP/ECP and EETs activate platelets, expose tissue factor, neutralize heparan sulfate and downregulate thrombomodulin.
Persistent tissue eosinophil necrosis nucleates extravascular palisading granulomas with central eosinophilic necrosis.
MPO-ANCA primed neutrophils degranulate against endothelium and undergo NETosis driving fibrinoid necrosis of small vessels.
Activity reflected in MPO-ANCA titer; positive in ~30-40% of EGPA, classically perinuclear (p-ANCA) pattern.
MPO-ANCA classically yields p-ANCA pattern on IIF.
Glomerular capillary necrosis with crescent formation in MPO-ANCA+ EGPA subset.
Ischemic injury to peripheral nerves via epineurial vessel vasculitis.
Small dermal vessel necrosis produces palpable purpura, nodules and urticaria-like rash.
Mesenteric small/medium-vessel vasculitis adds ischemic component to GI eosinophilic infiltration; drives bowel perforation/ischemia in severe FFS+ disease.
Alveolar capillary necrosis can produce diffuse alveolar hemorrhage in MPO-ANCA+ EGPA.
Loss of functional glomeruli drives rising creatinine; can progress to RPGN and dialysis without immunosuppression.
Glomerular capillary rupture produces dysmorphic hematuria and RBC casts.
Glomerular barrier disruption produces sub-nephrotic to nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Active sediment with dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts is the hallmark of crescentic GN.
Quantifies glomerular protein leak.
Crescentic GN drives AKI; serum creatinine >1.58 mg/dL is one FFS factor and worsens mortality.
Asymmetric multifocal sensorimotor deficits (foot drop from peroneal nerve, wrist drop from radial nerve, ulnar/median deficits) with painful onset.
Peripheral neurologic deficits dominate; CNS strokes are uncommon but possible.
Myocyte necrosis releases troponin; routine troponin screening recommended in all new EGPA.
Reduced LV function, intracavitary thrombus, restrictive physiology with EMF.
Subendocardial/transmural late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI is the most sensitive marker of subclinical involvement.
Late stage of unchecked eosinophilic infiltration is endomyocardial fibrosis with restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Myocyte necrosis is a defining FFS-positive feature.
Eosinophilic myocarditis with arrhythmia, heart failure, sudden death.
Mucosal infiltration plus mesenteric ischemia produce postprandial pain, diarrhea, GI bleeding.
Bowel wall thickening, mesenteric edema and small-bowel ulceration on CT/endoscopy.
Severe transmural ischemic ulceration leads to perforation; FFS-positive feature; surgical emergency with high mortality.
Transient migratory peripheral non-segmental opacities; ground-glass and consolidation patterns.
Productive/dry cough from airway and parenchymal eosinophilia.
Alveolar filling with eosinophilic exudate impairs gas exchange.
Severe adult-onset eosinophilic asthma is the prodromal hallmark, present in >95% of patients.
Severe asthma exacerbations with bronchospasm.
Bilateral nasal polyposis on rhinoscopy; chronic anosmia and obstruction.
Increased VTE/arterial thrombosis risk; intracardiac thrombus over fibrotic endocardium.
Cardioembolic stroke from intracardiac thrombus; less commonly cerebral vasculitis.
Alveolar capillary rupture produces hemoptysis (often modest relative to alveolar bleeding).
Catastrophic but rare in EGPA; mostly in MPO-ANCA+ subset.
Drop in hemoglobin from alveolar bleeding.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute phase response; CRP commonly markedly elevated.
Acute phase response with elevated ESR.
Low-grade fever common in vasculitic phase.
Cytokine-driven cachexia and anorexia.
Constitutional symptoms of active vasculitis.
Anemia of inflammation.
Reactive thrombocytosis is common in active vasculitis.
Palpable purpura on lower extremities is the most common cutaneous finding.
Subcutaneous nodules, urticaria-like lesions, livedo.
Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score sums organ-specific active features.
Cardiac involvement is one of five FFS components, each adding to mortality risk.
GI involvement is an FFS component.
Renal insufficiency (Cr >1.58 mg/dL or 150 µmol/L) is an FFS component.
Cardiac involvement is the leading single contributor to EGPA mortality (~50% of disease-related deaths).
Severe GI vasculitis with perforation/ischemia is a major mortality driver.
Renal failure adds to mortality directly and via cumulative organ damage.
DAH carries high acute mortality when present.
Cumulative steroid + cyclophosphamide/rituximab risk of bacterial sepsis, PJP, CMV, HBV, fungal infection, herpes zoster.
Treatment-related infection is a major non-disease mortality contributor, especially during induction.
Eosinophil neurotoxic granule proteins contribute to nerve injury independently of vasculitis, especially in ANCA-negative phenotype.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: requires eosinophilia >1.5x10^9/L for ACR/EULAR 2022 classification points
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Marked blood eosinophilia is a classification criterion (>1.0x10^9/L gives points; tissue eosinophilia, MPO-ANCA, and other criteria additive).

axes.shape_free_text: Markedly elevated at vasculitic phase, often >1.5x10^9/L (>10% of WBC); can exceed 5-10x10^9/L. Falls rapidly with corticosteroids (within days) and with mepolizumab.
Often elevated due to eosinophilia; total WBC 12-25 common.
Modest neutrophilia from acute phase response; rises further on glucocorticoids.
Often reduced during steroid induction.
Mild-moderate anemia of inflammation; severe drop only with DAH or GI bleeding.
Reactive thrombocytosis common (400-800).
Markedly elevated during vasculitic phase, often 50-200 mg/L. Responds promptly to glucocorticoids.
Markedly elevated, often >60 mm/hr; lags CRP.
Positive in ~30-40% of EGPA; titer often parallels glomerulonephritis/PNS/DAH activity. Negative in remainder (predominantly cardiac/eosinophilic phenotype).
Rarely positive in EGPA; if strongly positive, reconsider GPA.
p-ANCA pattern by IIF in MPO-ANCA+ subset.
Total IgE typically elevated, often 200-2000 IU/mL.
Usually normal in ANCA-negative phenotype; rises with crescentic GN.
Tracks creatinine in renal involvement.
Sub-nephrotic to nephrotic-range proteinuria with active GN.
Dysmorphic hematuria with RBC casts in active GN.
Active proteinuria.
Active sediment with dysmorphic RBCs/RBC casts in renal-active subset.
Often abnormal even in clinically silent cardiac involvement; routine screening recommended.
Reduced LVEF, regional wall motion abnormalities, intracavitary thrombus, restrictive physiology with EMF.
Subendocardial/transmural LGE on cardiac MRI is the most sensitive marker; persists after clinical recovery.
Late stage; restrictive physiology with apical obliteration and intracavitary thrombus.
Transient migratory non-segmental peripheral consolidation/ground-glass opacities on CT; resolves rapidly with steroids.
Bowel wall thickening, mesenteric edema, small-bowel ulceration on CT/endoscopy.
Asymmetric multifocal sensorimotor deficits with painful onset; foot drop, wrist drop most classic. Recovery slow and often incomplete (months to years).
Severe adult-onset asthma; near-universal prodrome; persists in remission.
Bilateral nasal polyposis on rhinoscopy with anosmia and obstruction; prodromal and persistent.
Lower-extremity palpable purpura.
Subcutaneous nodules, urticaria-like lesions, livedo reticularis.
Postprandial abdominal pain, GI bleeding, diarrhea in GI-active disease.
Cough from asthma and pulmonary infiltrates.
Modest in DAH; absent in pure eosinophilic pneumonia.
Pleuritic or anginal chest pain in cardiac/serositic involvement.
Peripheral neurologic deficits dominate (mononeuritis multiplex). CNS rare.
Constitutional fatigue.
Modest involuntary weight loss in active phase.
Low-grade fever common; high fever in concomitant infection.
Tachycardia in active inflammation; bradycardia or arrhythmia possible with myocarditis.
Often normal; hypotension only in fulminant cardiac involvement or sepsis.
May rise with renal involvement and steroid therapy.
Decreases with eosinophilic pneumonia or DAH.
Tachypnea with pulmonary involvement.
Decreased due to acute phase, nephrotic-range proteinuria, GI losses.
Mildly elevated in active disease or with hepatic eosinophilic infiltration.
Mild elevation; can be markedly elevated with myocarditis or rhabdomyolysis component.
Can be elevated in eosinophilic myositis or cardiac involvement.
Elevated in active vasculitis and prothrombotic state.
Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score capturing organ-specific active features.

Five-Factor Score (revised 2009): age >65, cardiac involvement, GI involvement, renal insufficiency (Cr >150 µmol/L), absence of ENT symptoms; each = 1 point. FFS ≥1 prompts cyclophosphamide-based induction.
Increased with crescentic GN.
Low absolute risk but high lethality when present, mostly in MPO-ANCA+ subset.
Cardiac involvement is FFS-positive; subclinical injury common.
Eosinophilic myocarditis with arrhythmia, heart failure, sudden death.
Increased VTE/arterial thrombosis risk.
Cardioembolic stroke risk from intracardiac thrombus over fibrotic endocardium.
Rare; from CNS vasculitis or anticoagulation in DAH.
Severe asthma exacerbations.
Severe transmural ischemic ulceration in mesenteric vasculitis. Surgical emergency, high mortality.
Treatment-emergent infection during induction is a major mortality contributor.
Risk on steroid taper after prolonged supraphysiologic dosing.

Aggregate mortality hazard. Untreated severe FFS+ disease historically ≥50% 5-year mortality; with modern induction 5-year survival ~85-90%. Cardiac involvement is the dominant single cause of disease death.
Cumulative immunosuppression load.
Highest with rituximab; requires HBV serology screening before induction.
Screen with IGRA, HBV/HCV serology before high-dose steroids/cyclophosphamide/rituximab.
High with cumulative cyclophosphamide >7-10 g; favors rituximab in fertility-relevant patients.
Contraindicates cyclophosphamide and methotrexate; mycophenolate teratogenic; favors steroids ± azathioprine.
Steroid-emergent psychiatric symptoms, hyperglycemia, osteoporosis, weight gain, hypertension.
Frequent on glucocorticoids; contributes to LV strain in cardiac-active disease.
Requires dose adjustment of cyclophosphamide.
MPO-ANCA+ subset (~30-40%): more renal/PNS/DAH, more cyclophosphamide/rituximab benefit; ANCA-negative subset: more cardiac/eosinophilic phenotype, more mepolizumab benefit.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Blood eosinophilia is the most direct surrogate of Th2/IL-5 activity.
Both reflect IL-6-driven acute phase response; CRP rises and falls faster.
Both result from glomerular injury in pauci-immune crescentic GN.
Active myocyte necrosis precedes detectable LGE on cardiac MRI by days to weeks.
Persistent peripheral eosinophilia is a risk factor for cardiac infiltration.
MPO-ANCA+ subset has substantially higher GN, PNS, DAH probability than ANCA-negative.
Untreated active eosinophilic myocarditis evolves to endomyocardial fibrosis with restrictive cardiomyopathy.
Cumulative immunosuppression dose drives infection hazard.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Pulse steroids (250-1000 mg/day x 3) standard for severe organ-threatening EGPA (cardiac, renal, GI, DAH, severe PNS).
Acute high-dose can precipitate psychosis, hyperglycemia.
Active uncontrolled infection requires concurrent treatment; steroids may still be needed but with antimicrobial coverage.

treatments.context_specific_role: Initial induction in severe organ-threatening EGPA (FFS≥1, cardiac/renal/GI/PNS/DAH); typically 500-1000 mg/day x 3 days, then transition to oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cumulative steroid exposure drives diabetes, osteoporosis, cataracts, infection.
Screen and prophylax.

treatments.context_specific_role: Backbone of induction (1 mg/kg/day) and maintenance (taper to 5-7.5 mg/day). Standalone may be sufficient for non-severe (FFS=0) disease; combined with steroid-sparing agent for severe disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Indicated when FFS≥1 (cardiac, GI, renal, severe PNS, CNS, DAH).
Teratogenic and gonadotoxic.
Limit cumulative dose; consider rituximab alternative.
Reduce dose; mesna protection mandatory.

treatments.context_specific_role: Induction for severe organ-threatening EGPA (FFS≥1). Typical CYCLOPS regimen (15 mg/kg IV every 2-3 weeks x 3-6 doses) with mesna; PJP prophylaxis required. Followed by maintenance (azathioprine, methotrexate, or rituximab).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ANCA+ phenotype shows comparable efficacy to cyclophosphamide; less robust evidence in ANCA-negative phenotype.
Preferred over CYC in fertility-relevant patients.
Risk of HBV reactivation; screen and prophylax with entecavir/tenofovir if HBcAb+.

failure_modes: incomplete eosinophil suppression in ANCA-negative disease
treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative induction in severe ANCA+ EGPA, especially when cyclophosphamide is contraindicated (fertility, prior CYC, malignancy concerns). Also used for relapse and as maintenance (every 6 months).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Higher baseline eosinophilia predicts greater response.
Particularly effective for asthma/sinonasal/eosinophilic features.
Not validated for FFS≥1 organ-threatening induction; reserve for non-severe relapsing/refractory or steroid-sparing maintenance.

failure_modes: need for concurrent steroid for vasculitic features

side_effects.interpretation: Modest; mild URTI most common; helminth infection theoretical risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Approved (300 mg SC every 4 weeks) for relapsing/refractory non-severe EGPA and as steroid-sparing maintenance. Strongest benefit in asthma, sinonasal, eosinophilic phenotype, especially ANCA-negative subset.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Compatible with pregnancy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Maintenance therapy after CYC induction (typically 2 mg/kg/day); pregnancy-compatible.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Teratogenic; abortifacient.
Accumulates in renal failure.
Inferior to CYC for severe induction; reserve for non-severe disease and maintenance.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative for non-severe induction (FFS=0) or maintenance after CYC induction. Avoid in pregnancy and CKD.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Teratogenic.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative maintenance therapy when azathioprine intolerant.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Selected use for severe DAH or co-existing anti-GBM disease, despite negative PEXIVAS findings for routine AAV.

treatments.context_specific_role: Selected use only: severe DAH refractory to steroids/immunosuppression, or co-existing anti-GBM disease. Routine use not supported in AAV after PEXIVAS.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Useful when standard immunosuppression must be withheld due to infection.
Pregnancy-compatible adjunctive option.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adjunctive for refractory neuropathy, during severe infection, or in pregnancy when standard immunosuppression unsafe.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Foundational asthma controller therapy in EGPA.

treatments.context_specific_role: Lifelong maintenance for eosinophilic asthma component; reduces exacerbations and steroid burden.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Lymphopenia <500-800 on steroids/CYC/RTX warrants PJP prophylaxis.
Hemolysis risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: PJP prophylaxis throughout induction with high-dose steroids + CYC/RTX, especially with lymphopenia. Standard in severe EGPA induction.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active alveolar bleeding.
Active bleeding contraindication.

treatments.context_specific_role: For documented intracardiac thrombus, VTE, or arterial thromboembolism in EGPA. Duration 3-6 months minimum, longer with persistent EMF/thrombus.

positive.trajectory_modulation: Higher rates of glomerulonephritis, mononeuritis multiplex, alveolar hemorrhage, purpura. Lower rates of cardiac involvement.

negative.trajectory_modulation: Higher rates of cardiac involvement, eosinophilic infiltrative phenotype, fewer renal/PNS features. Better mepolizumab response.

present.trajectory_modulation: Near-universal prerequisite (>95%); typically precedes vasculitis by 4-10 years.
Common ENT prodrome; absence is one FFS factor (worsens prognosis).

recent_exposure.trajectory_modulation: Controversial unmasking vs trigger relationship; probably mostly steroid-sparing unmasking of pre-existing EGPA.

recent_taper.trajectory_modulation: Common relapse trigger; flares often occur during taper below 7.5 mg prednisolone.

elderly.trajectory_modulation: Age >65 is one FFS factor; worse prognosis and treatment tolerability.

supportive_care: Five-Factor Score (FFS) calculation at diagnosis (cardiac, GI, renal, age >65, absence of ENT)
Cardiac screening at diagnosis: 12-lead ECG, troponin, NT-proBNP, transthoracic echocardiogram, low threshold for cardiac MRI even when asymptomatic
Quantify mononeuritis multiplex with detailed neurologic exam; nerve conduction studies
Baseline pulmonary function tests and high-resolution chest CT
Renal: urinalysis, urine sediment, urine protein/creatinine ratio, serum creatinine; nephrology referral if active sediment
Skin/nerve/lung biopsy for histologic confirmation when accessible
ANCA testing (MPO and PR3 by ELISA plus IIF) and total IgE at diagnosis
Pre-induction screening: HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV, latent TB (IGRA), strongyloides serology in endemic exposure, varicella status
TPMT/NUDT15 genotype before azathioprine
PJP prophylaxis (TMP-SMX) during induction with high-dose steroids plus CYC or rituximab; until lymphocytes recover and steroid <20 mg
Bone protection: calcium, vitamin D, bisphosphonate or denosumab if prolonged steroid use
Vaccination: inactivated influenza annually, pneumococcal (PCV13/PCV20 then PPSV23), recombinant zoster vaccine; avoid live vaccines on immunosuppression
Tight glycemic control during steroid therapy; HbA1c monitoring
Blood pressure monitoring and management
Fertility counseling before cyclophosphamide; gamete preservation when feasible
Contraception during cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, and mycophenolate
Asthma controller optimization with ICS/LABA throughout disease course
Cardiac rehabilitation and heart failure management when myocarditis/EMF present
Physiotherapy and occupational therapy for mononeuritis multiplex recovery
Pain management for vasculitic neuropathy (gabapentinoids, duloxetine)
Disease activity tracking with BVAS at each visit; relapse monitoring with eosinophil count, CRP, ANCA, urinalysis
Patient education on relapse warning signs (rising eosinophils, asthma worsening, new neuropathy, purpura, hematuria)
Multidisciplinary care: rheumatology, pulmonology, cardiology, nephrology, neurology, ENT, ophthalmology as needed
